Kernels and scales of effect

Source: R/doc_kernels.R
multiScaleR-kernels.Rd

multiScaleR summarizes the landscape around each survey point with a kernel, a function that gives nearby raster cells more weight than distant ones. The width of the kernel is its scale parameter, sigma, measured in map units. This page defines the four kernel families, explains which covariates use smooth kernel weights and which use a hard radius, shows how sigma is converted into a distance you can report, and explains how to choose max_D. For worked examples, see the section "Understand the kernel and its parameters" in vignette("v02-user-guide", package = "multiScaleR").

What a kernel does

The scale of effect is the distance over which a landscape variable influences a response measured at a survey point. Instead of fitting one model per buffer radius, multiScaleR weights every raster cell around a point by its distance and estimates the kernel width from your data, along with the regression coefficients.

For a survey point and a raster layer, kernel_prep() extracts the cells within max_D map units of the point and records the distance d from the point to each cell center. A kernel-weighted covariate is then the weighted mean of those cell values v:

$$x = \frac{\sum_i w(d_i) v_i}{\sum_i w(d_i)}$$

The sums run over cells with a finite value. A missing cell drops out of both sums, so the remaining weights renormalize. Because the weight function appears above and below the line, any normalizing constant cancels and only the shape of w(d) matters. The model then uses this covariate after centering and scaling, as described in kernel_prep().

Sigma is estimated by multiScale_optim() (or multiScale_bayes()). It is always in the linear units of the projection, usually meters.

Choose a kernel family

Set the kernel with the kernel argument of kernel_prep(). All covariates prepared together share one kernel, so comparing kernels means one kernel_prep() call per kernel. The weight functions below come from the package code.

Kernelkernel =Weight of a cell at distance dEstimated parameters
Gaussian (default)"gaussian"exp(-d^2 / (2 * sigma^2))sigma
Negative exponential"exp"exp(-d / sigma)sigma
Exponential power"expow"exp(-(d / sigma)^shape)sigma and shape
Fixed buffer"fixed"1 when d < sigma, 0 otherwisesigma, which is the buffer radius

How to read the parameters:

  • Gaussian. Sigma is the standard deviation of a normal curve. A cell at distance sigma gets about 61% of the weight of a cell at the point, and a cell at twice sigma gets about 14%.

  • Negative exponential. Sigma is the decay length. A cell at distance sigma gets about 37% (1/e) of the weight at the point. The weight drops faster near the point than under a Gaussian kernel and has a longer tail.

  • Exponential power. A cell at distance sigma always gets about 37% of the weight at the point, and shape sets the form of the curve. With shape = 1 the kernel is the negative exponential with the same sigma. With shape = 2 it has the Gaussian form, with a standard deviation of sigma / sqrt(2). Larger values flatten the top and steepen the edge, so the kernel approaches a fixed buffer of radius sigma. Values below 1 give a sharper peak and a heavier tail. kernel_prep() starts the shape at 2, and the default refit search of multiScale_optim() keeps it between 0.75 and 50.

  • Fixed buffer. Every cell whose center lies within sigma gets equal weight, so the covariate is the plain mean of those cells.

Start with the Gaussian kernel. Fit the other kernels when you have a reason to test a different decay shape, and compare the fits by AICc with aic_tab(). Not every fitting route accepts every kernel, as multiScaleR-fitting-methods explains.

Smooth kernels and hard radii

A covariate's scale is either a smooth kernel width or a hard radius, and the two behave differently during estimation.

Smooth kernel weights. Kernel means from kernel_var() and kernel-weighted surface metrics from surface_var(..., weighted = TRUE) use the Gaussian, negative exponential, or exponential power weights above. Each weight changes continuously with sigma, so the likelihood is a smooth function of sigma. multiScale_optim() can then report a Hessian-based (Wald) standard error and confidence interval for sigma.

Hard radius. Some covariates count each cell fully or not at all:

  • Every landscape metric from landscape_var().

  • Every surface metric from surface_var() with weighted = FALSE (the default).

  • Every optimized covariate prepared with kernel = "fixed", including kernel means and weighted surface metrics.

The estimated scale of such a covariate is a radius in map units. The covariate changes only when the radius passes the distance of a cell center, so the likelihood is a step function of the radius. It is flat between steps and jumps at them, which leaves no useful curvature for a Hessian standard error. The default summary therefore shows NA for the standard error and Wald interval of a hard radius. Examine the likelihood profile instead, with profile_sigma() or summary(fit, profile = TRUE), and report the estimate as a radius in map units. An interval read from a profile cutoff does not by itself establish coverage for a stepped likelihood. Because a flat objective can stall a search at its start, multiScale_optim() screens several starting values by default when the kernel is "fixed".

Under kernel = "expow", a hard-radius covariate has no shape parameter. Its reported shape and shape standard error are NA, and model selection leaves that unused position out of the parameter count.

A metric given a fixed radius in landscape_var() or surface_var() has no scale to estimate. It is computed once and enters the model as an ordinary covariate.

Report an effective distance

Sigma is a parameter, not a radius. The same sigma reaches a different distance under each kernel, so report an effective distance, the distance that holds a stated share prob of the kernel weight (90% by default). kernel_dist() makes the conversion, plot_kernel() draws it, and summary() of a fitted model reports it next to each sigma.

Two definitions are available through the dimension argument:

  • Planar, dimension = "2d" (the default since version 0.7.4). Raster cells lie on a plane, and the number of cells at distance d grows with the circumference 2 pi d. The planar distance is the radius of the circle around the point that holds prob of the total kernel weight. Use it when you describe the area a kernel draws on.

  • Line-based, dimension = "1d". The kernel is treated as a curve along a single transect through the point. The distance encloses prob of the area under that curve. This was the default before version 0.7.4.

KernelLine-based distance ("1d")Planar radius ("2d")At prob = 0.9, 1D and 2D
Gaussianqnorm((1 + prob) / 2) * sigmasigma * sqrt(-2 * log(1 - prob))1.645 and 2.146 times sigma
Negative exponential-sigma * log(1 - prob)sigma * qgamma(prob, shape = 2)2.303 and 3.890 times sigma
Exponential powersigma * qgamma(prob, shape = 1 / shape)^(1 / shape)sigma * qgamma(prob, shape = 2 / shape)^(1 / shape)Depends on shape
Fixed buffersigma * probsigma * sqrt(prob)0.900 and 0.949 times sigma

For example, a Gaussian kernel with sigma = 300 m holds 90% of its planar weight within about 644 m, while the line-based 90% distance is about 493 m. On an unbounded plane, the circle of radius 493 m holds only about 74% of the weight. A hard-radius covariate reports its radius under either definition. Always state the definition and the share of weight you report.

Both definitions describe the ideal, continuous kernel on an unbounded plane. They ignore truncation at max_D, raster edges, missing cells, and cell geometry, so the share of weight held by the cells actually extracted around a point can differ. The pct_wt smoothing window of kernel_scale.raster(), the default max_D of sim_dat(), and the max_D warning of multiScale_optim() keep the line-based definition.

Choose max_D

max_D, set in kernel_prep(), does three jobs.

  • It sets the neighborhood. Each point gets every raster cell that intersects a circle of radius max_D around it, including partly covered cells at the edge, which keep their full kernel weight. Cells beyond max_D are never seen, so each kernel is cut off at max_D and its weights renormalize over the extracted cells.

  • It bounds the search. multiScale_optim() estimates sigma, or a hard radius, between min_D (the spacing of adjacent cell centers, about one cell width) and max_D. multiScale_bayes() places priors on sigma without these hard bounds, but its covariates still use only the cells extracted within max_D.

  • It sets the cost. A larger max_D extracts more cells per point, which costs preparation time and memory. With bin = TRUE (the default) the cost of optimizing kernel means no longer depends on max_D. The raster must cover each point's full buffer.

Set max_D above the largest scale you consider plausible. After fitting, multiScale_optim() flags an estimate whose line-based 90% distance is more than half of max_D. It prints a warning (when verbose = TRUE), records the max_distance entry of diagnostics(), and suggests a larger max_D in its next_run element. For a Gaussian kernel the flag appears once sigma exceeds about max_D / 3.3, and for a negative exponential kernel once it exceeds about max_D / 4.6. So for a plausible upper sigma s, choose max_D of at least 3.3 s (Gaussian) or 4.6 s (negative exponential). Also compare the planar radius from kernel_dist(sigma = s, kernel = ...) with max_D. When that radius approaches max_D, the extracted cells hold noticeably less of the kernel weight than the ideal kernel describes. If an estimate comes back near max_D, increase max_D, run kernel_prep() again, and refit. Do not shrink a scientifically chosen max_D only to save memory. estimate_multiscale_ram() describes leaner preparation options.

Functions that use kernels

FunctionWhat it does with the kernel
kernel_prep(), kernel_prep_by_group()Set the kernel and max_D, and extract cells and distances
msr_vars()Declare kernel means, kernel-weighted surface metrics, and hard-radius metrics
multiScale_optim()Estimate sigma (and shape) with the model
kernel_dist()Convert sigma into an effective distance
plot_kernel()Draw a kernel without a fitted model
profile_sigma()Trace the likelihood across sigma or a hard radius
kernel_scale.raster()Apply fitted kernels to whole rasters for mapping
sim_dat()Simulate responses at known scales of effect
